articles.title: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
articles.summary: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including a photojournalist working for The Washington Post.
body: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.
The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital. "We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground." She said "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also tore her cameras and phone off her.
She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement Levine has received medical care and is safe.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.
Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."
The Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to gather their olive harvest. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.
At least six people were injured in two attacks in the West Bank town of Abu Falah, outside Ramallah, on Friday, The Associated Press reported citing the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another attack earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh, as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah of the Committee to Protect Journalists said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said. She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities have failed to stop them.

articles.title: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests
articles.summary: Protests have intensified over a review of voter lists that critics say is politically motivated and threatens to disenfranchise voters. The Election Commission and Modi's administration deny these allegations.
body: NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.

Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.
The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.
The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.

Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.

Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.

A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.
"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.

The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.

articles.title: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
articles.summary: The Irish author said her books can no longer be sold in the UK after she pledged the royalties to a banned pro-Palestinian group.
body: Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.

Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.

In a statement this week, her publisher explained: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.

The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.
Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.

UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."

It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.

Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media, Trump called those responsible "terrorists."

When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.

"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.

The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."
But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.
U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."

"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.
Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."
Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.
For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.
But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."
Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.

The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.

The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.
In August, the U.S. Department of the Treasury followed the UK's lead in sanctioning Palestinian Action, calling them "far-left terrorists."

articles.title: Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric
articles.summary: Social Security benefits are set to get a boost to offset rising consumer prices. And, streamer Hasan Piker says the GOP's "guilt-by-association politics" won't drag Democrats down in the midterms.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Consumer prices in September were 3.7% higher than they were a year ago, according to a Labor Department report. A spike in energy prices linked to the U.S. war with Iran drove up the cost of living. Excluding energy and food prices, core inflation reached 2.6% in September, up from August. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits for next year after the release of the inflation report. This annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices from July, August and September. Some recipients say the increase is not enough.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced he will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries, despite President Trump's request to refrain from doing so. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that he had ordered commanders to stand down earlier this week, but wouldn't anymore. But Ukraine's ability to conduct these long-range attacks may be limited, as it has seen sudden crippling restrictions to Starshield, the satellite communications system provided by the U.S.

A man shot and wounded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in New York last week says he didn't know the men who shot him were ICE agents until after he woke up in the hospital. A new petition filed in Brooklyn federal court says the agents — many of them masked — didn't identify themselves before approaching Oscar Belgal's vehicle with their firearms drawn. The filing contradicts the Trump administration's version of events.

Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.

California-based Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has emerged as a key target for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections. The president recently labeled him a "terrible liability" and a "communist." In Michigan, political ads attempting to link him to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayef repeatedly play Piker's most controversial statements, including the infamous "America deserved 9/11." Piker remains confident that he won't hinder Democrats this November. In a conversation with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, he reflects on his past remarks, the loneliness young men feel and his critique of Tucker Carlson.
Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.

Australian DJ Lenny Pearce is taking over venues with his toddler rave world tour. Yes, it's is exactly what it sounds like: techno dance parties for families. Most of the dance floor is filled with little ones under the age of five. Around 5 p.m., the speakers blast nursery rhymes like "Bingo" and "The Wheels on the Bus," while the bar offers a refreshing house specialty: apple juice. Pearce kicked off the North American leg of his tour in Baltimore, but has sold-out shows in cities such as New York and Los Angeles and has already captivated audiences in Bahrain, Singapore and India. Take a look at these photos of the young ravers at his events.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over.
body: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.

The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.

Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.

The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.

Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.

"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.

Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.

"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

articles.title: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training
articles.summary: One plays the bull, the other the bullfighter, as a pair practices a dance of death in a sport that's prohibited in the Mexican capital city.
body: They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.
"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.
"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.
"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."
The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.

As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."
Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.

articles.title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back on front line where Starlink plays a key role
articles.summary: The BBC joins Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi as it regains crucial territory in the Donbas, but optimism has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump.
body: Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.
The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warning

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas region

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front line
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from drones
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

articles.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
articles.summary: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.
body: Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.
Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.
Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.
The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

articles.title: Zelensky rallies EU support as Trump says Ukraine leader 'more difficult to deal with than Putin'
articles.summary: The US president launches a new wave of blistering criticism at Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels.
body: Zelensky arrived at a summit in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen
US President Donald Trump has renewed his sharp criticism of Volodymyr Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader is "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".
Trump, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import its diesel to the American market, called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace".
Zelensky had paused the attacks for three days at Trump's request for a ceasefire on energy targets, but said on Thursday they would resume because Moscow had never stopped.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated recently over the US-Russia diesel deal and restrictions on Ukraine's satellite communications on the battlefield.
Zelensky has not commented on Trump's latest criticism, however thanked "real leaders" for their support as he arrived at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
He was flanked by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

"Of course we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire but we've seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute," Von der Leyen told reporters, adding that sanctions on Russia "have to increase".
Moscow said it had never agreed to the energy ceasefire that Trump suddenly announced last week.

Costa did not mention the US, but said that "this is no time to withdraw support" to the country and "no time to relieve Russian sanctions", as the US has done in agreeing to the deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
The summit's agenda focuses on funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another cold winter - the fifth since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

"Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure," Von der Leyen told Zelensky before the summit began, "but we stand by your side, we support you as we did in the other winters."
Zelensky said his country wants the war to end "as quick as possible", but added that Russia is not showing signs that it wants the same thing.
"That's why we have to prepare for the winter. A winter package is not only energy, it's also defence and funding," he said.

Deadly attacks on Ukraine continued overnight, with several people killed in a Russian drone strike in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, while some 270,000 households were without power after strikes in the western Volyn region, the local governors said.
A member of Ukraine's emergency service sifts through rubble at the scene of a Russian drone strike in the north-western Rivne region
Trump's comments about Zelensky, during an interview with US outlet Newsmax on Thursday evening, reflect the deteriorating relationship between the US and Ukraine.
The US president said he is "not a big fan of Zelensky" and that he is "not a good guy for us to deal with.
"He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't," Trump said.
"As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin," he added. "And when you have that kind of hatred, it's very hard to get something settled."
When asked about Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries, Trump said it was "a disgrace".
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher... There are a lot of targets that you can hit."

Trump is frustrated at Ukraine's continued targeting of Russian oil refineries because it affects Moscow's ability to export its diesel to America, as per the deal the US recently made with Russia, in an effort to bring down fuel prices.

Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, souring Trump standing with the American public - something he wants to fix before next month's mid-term elections.
The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin and an "investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
His anger was further heightened earlier this week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.

On Tuesday night, when the communications network was limited, there were several deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning of the incoming attack.
The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence sharing - which is crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.
Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
Zelensky has been holding back-to-back talks with EU leaders while in Brussels. On Thursday he met Nato chief Marke Rutte, as well as the leaders of Poland, France, Denmark and Belgium.
A day earlier, he met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at No 10 in London.
At the summit on Friday, Zelensky also held talks with the chiefs of the European Council and European Commission, and was set to meet the prime ministers of Hungary, Finland, and Sweden.
Supporting Ukraine through another freezing winter is high on the agenda at the summit in Brussels

Ukraine also continued its strikes against Russia overnight. The airspace above Moscow was closed for several house, causing flight delays, as 644 drones were intercepted above 26 Russian regions, the defence ministry said.
Ninety-four Ukrainian drones were shot down as they approached Moscow, the mayor said.
In the Vladimir region, east of Moscow, the governor said that Ukrainian drones were intercepted to prevent an attack on heating infrastructure in the area.
And the governor of the southern Rostov region said that Ukrainian drones hit industrial and warehouse facilities, causing a fire and injuring one person.

articles.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.
body: Pope Leo thanked medical staff as he was pictured for the first time since his lung surgery
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers

Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says

articles.title: India's 'cockroach' party founder detained ahead of protest
articles.summary: The youth-led movement had called for a Delhi protest after mass detentions last week and the jailing of two leaders.
body: Abhijeet Dipke's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has drawn thousands onto the streets in recent months
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's "cockroach" movement, and a few others were detained in Delhi as police tried to stop a protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.
Hundreds had gathered in Connaught Place, one of the capital's busiest commercial districts, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans despite a heavy security presence.
Police sealed off Central Park, the planned site of the protest, and deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent the gathering.
The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) accuses India's Election Commission of manipulating voter lists to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP. Both deny the allegation.

The group has held a series of protests in Delhi in recent weeks, with police repeatedly detaining its leaders and supporters. Friday's demonstration unfolded under similarly heavy security presence, though the police response was more restrained than during last weekend's sweeping crackdown.

Hours before the protest, police went to the house where Dipke was staying. In an exchange broadcast live on Instagram, he challenged officers who had come to caution him against holding the march, asking whether waving the Indian flag was against the law.
Hours later, the BBC saw officers surround Dipke as he approached his car and force him into a police vehicle. Some supporters tried to stop it from leaving.

It was Dipke's second detention in less than a week. Last Saturday, police had boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi to prevent him from reaching another demonstration. He was released the following day.

The movement's two other main leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were also detained last weekend and later released. But on Wednesday, they were sent to jail for five days after returning to Jantar Mantar, a protest site near parliament that police had recently declared off-limits. Friday's march was partly intended to demand the release of Das and Ranka.
Dipke's detention means the movement's three main leaders are once again in custody.
The CJP said it had lost contact with him and accused police of taking him to an undisclosed location and denying him access to lawyers.

But they insist the arrests and detentions will not stop them. "They may detain three people, but how will they stop 30 tomorrow? How will they stop 300 leaders?" CJP spokesperson Mehr Pasricha told the BBC.
Police have not publicly confirmed the grounds for Dipke's detention or responded to the CJP's latest allegations.
Anish Gawande, the opposition politician who had been hosting Dipke, also questioned the police action.
"Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," he said.
Hundreds of people gathered in central Delhi to unfurl the national flag as part of the protest
At Connaught Place, the police presence dwarfed the protest itself.

Around 200-300 people initially gathered outside Central Park, which authorities had closed. Unable to enter, they walked around its perimeter, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans. More protesters arrived as the evening progressed.
Officers kept emerging from buses parked around the district. Journalists crowded the streets too, and together with police, they far outnumbered the demonstrators.
For much of the evening, police largely held back, with the BBC witnessing only a handful of detentions. But as darkness fell, officers began using force against some protesters.
The BBC saw some young demonstrators being pushed into a bus where women were already being held. Inside were around 50 female officers, far more than the number of detainees.
The BBC also saw two people being injured during the police action. One protester fell to the ground and appeared to have hurt their leg.

Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She had also been detained during last weekend's crackdown.
Student activist Neha Bora is among the people detained by the Delhi police on Friday evening

Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.

By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked exam papers. A march towards parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister.

The CJP has since turned its attention to India's electoral system, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sweeping revision of voter lists known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).

Critics say the exercise risks removing legitimate voters from the rolls, potentially depriving them of the right to vote. The Election Commission says it is targeting ineligible, dead and duplicate voters and denies allegations that it is favouring the ruling BJP.

Last weekend, authorities imposed severe restrictions to stop CJP supporters from reaching a planned rally, sealing off roads, shutting metro stations and deploying thousands of security personnel across Delhi.
The BBC witnessed, external dozens of protesters being detained across the capital, including students and journalists.
The action drew criticism but police defended it as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were released the following day after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. But the dispute over where they could protest was only beginning.
Delhi authorities have said Central Park is closed on Friday and Saturday for "administrative reasons"
Police removed Jantar Mantar from Delhi's list of approved protest sites, naming three alternative venues.

Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory stands close to Parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused authorities of trying to push demonstrations away from the seat of power.
On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned to the restricted site with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar.
Police said some protesters had climbed over a locked gate and that the organisers had breached the conditions of their release. The following day, the two men were sent to jail for five days.
The arrests did little to deter the movement from announcing another demonstration.
In a video message on Thursday, Dipke urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities. He also acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again.
"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said.
By Friday morning, police had served him with a notice warning against holding the march without permission.
Authorities closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons", and offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location.
The CJP came up with a different plan. Supporters were told to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave.
"Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the movement declared in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour. It urged supporters to share their photographs online.
Sporadic protests erupted around the Central Park on Friday evening despite the detentions
Opposition parties have also been holding protests against Kumar and the Election Commission.

Last week, Rahul Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were detained while attempting to march to the commission's headquarters. They have also taken their concerns to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.
Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP leaders and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to protesters, although the opposition and the youth-led movement have largely demonstrated separately.
Home Minister Amit Shah has accused the opposition of spreading falsehoods about the voter-list revision and defended the commission's independence.
For the CJP, the immediate question is how long it can sustain its protests with its three main leaders in custody.
Pasricha said the party had a team and a plan in place. "If the top three continue to stay behind bars, we will continue to protest peacefully," she said.

articles.title: US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions
articles.summary: Ukraine says temporary speed limits to the Starlink internet network disrupted its battlefield missions.
body: Democratic Party Senator Jeanne Shaheen has spearheaded the cross-party statement from several US senators
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into disruptions to SpaceX's Starlink internet network in Ukraine.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said it had unexpectedly restricted how fast drones could fly while maintaining internet connection.
In the letter, sent to the US defence department inspector general, the senators express "grave concern" about reports of speed curbs between 12 and 14 October.
Asked whether the US might have had a role in the slowdown, a US official told the BBC "no such request was ever made by the president [Donald Trump]".

The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen - a Democrat on the Senate's Foreign Relations Committee - calls for the inspector general to find out whether the restrictions were caused by the US defence department or its contractors.
It says "restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure".
Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
On Friday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told a news conference in Brussels that Starlink services were still being restored in his country.
"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," he said.
The senators also say they are "deeply concerned" by reports of disruptions or "glitches" affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine.
"We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement says.
"Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation," the senators add.

The letter's signatories include Republican Senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Cornyn, alongside Senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal and Christopher Coons from the Democrats.
Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
SpaceX owner Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind restrictions.
On Wednesday Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".

Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas. Starshield, which relies on the Starlink network, is designed for government and military use. Both are owned by Musk's SpaceX.
Zelensky has accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks against Russian energy sites.
On Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine's attacks would continue after Russia had continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure during an "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday.

Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days and would agree to the "energy ceasefire" if Moscow also abided by it. However, he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced.
The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal and Russia said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied.

Zelensky has also criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.

That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.

articles.title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
articles.summary: Joshua Foster "lost control" of his son while showing him the view of a water park from a window.
body: A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
The auditor, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
The incident happened on the first day of the family's holiday at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards an elevator and was playing with his son, said his lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou.
The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react.
Alexandrou told an earlier hearing, which took place on October 6, that Foster's life "changed forever" from that moment.
Police were called to reports of a child falling "under unknown circumstances" at about 18:40.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.
Alexandrou said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85m (9.3ft) wide and 1.2m (3.9ft) high.
Alexandros Alexandrou said his client's remorse was "clear"
In a statement outside court, Alexandrou described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."
He added Foster was "very emotional" after the sentencing and the family needed time to grieve properly.
"They have been in a defence mode during this procedure," Alexandrou said.

articles.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
articles.summary: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
body: The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.

About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.

The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.

So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.

Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale

articles.title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
articles.summary: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
body: Tirana has seen four days of clashes and the protests are spreading
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
There have been violent scenes involving protesters and police in central Tirana

Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.

The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
For almost five months over the summer, Albanians carrying images of flamingoes called on the prime minister to resign
Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania
'Flamingo Revolution' takes off as thousands demand Albanian PM's resignation
Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania

The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.

The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.

Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."

Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.

"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.

"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.

The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

articles.title: Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
articles.summary: Some of the 200 patients were found with "sores all over their bodies" and in overcrowded rooms.
body: Officials uncovered "gross inhuman conditions" when they raided the centre
A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.
The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.
Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".
Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.
Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.

Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg.
A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre.
Two minors were among the 200 people found living in crowded rooms at the facility
The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women.
The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water.
"Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said.
Gift Skhosana, one of those held at the facility, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika it was "common practice" for patients to be chained.
"They chain us as punishment [and] when you gain entry," he said.
Despite this, Skhosana, who was a drug user, said the facility helped him get clean and overcome his addiction.
Another person, who was not named, said his experience with the facility left him needing help mentally.
The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; £137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church.
Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said.
Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families.
The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday.
